headline: US-Iran conflict intensifies as Alphabet and Microsoft earnings loom tonight — ASX held firm while gold hits record $4,075 USD and your GXAI and PLS continue to drag on the portfolio.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Strong session for emerging markets today, lifted by a rising Aussie dollar (now 70.2 US cents) and positive sentiment around Chinese tech and trade. Still a small overall loss on cost, but today was a good day.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: AI enthusiasm gave GXAI a solid bump today — up 2.07% at the close. The broader AI sector got a boost from anticipation of strong cloud and AI results from Alphabet and Microsoft, both reporting earnings tonight US time. Still sitting at a -16.6% overall loss, but today's move is encouraging.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara slipped another 1.67% today as lithium prices remain under sustained pressure. Supply is recovering faster than demand, with analysts noting bearish pressure building before any potential next rally. The long-term thesis for lithium is intact, but the near-term pain continues — PLS is now down nearly 39% on what you paid.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Barely moved today — up just 0.09%. VDHG is a diversified set-and-forget fund, so quiet days like this are perfectly normal. No news, no drama.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: Essentially flat today — down just 0.04%. VTS tracks the entire US share market and often moves with overnight US moves, so last night's marginally softer S&P 500 (-0.19%) kept it steady. The overall position is slightly in the green at +1.85%.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG rose 1.52% in last night's session as investors built positions ahead of Q2 earnings due tonight US time. Strong search and cloud growth are expected. The co-founders reportedly had their fortunes jump by $15 billion on the rally — the market is optimistic.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft was the strongest US mover last night, up 2.15%, as markets got excited about Q4 earnings due tonight. Azure cloud growth and AI spending are the big focal points. Despite a strong night, your MSFT position is still down about 9.2% overall — you bought in at a higher price.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two edged up 0.97% last night in a generally positive session for NASDAQ stocks. No specific news overnight — just riding the broader tech wave. Your position is up about 2.9% overall.

watch_today.title: 🔴 Alphabet (GOOG) earnings tonight — big moment
watch_today.detail: Google's parent Alphabet reports Q2 2026 earnings tonight US time (after the bell, so early Wednesday AEST). The market is expecting strong search revenue and Google Cloud growth to justify the recent rally to $351. If they miss, expect a sharp move down. If they beat, your GOOG holding gets a nice boost. Worth watching Wednesday morning.

watch_today.title: 🔴 Microsoft (MSFT) earnings tonight — Azure growth in spotlight
watch_today.detail: Microsoft also reports Q4 2026 results tonight US time. The market wants to see Azure cloud growth and evidence that massive AI investment is converting into revenue. MSFT is up 2.15% ahead of results but is still down 9.2% on your cost — a strong beat could make meaningful inroads into that loss. Hold and see what tonight brings.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — lithium pain continues, but don't panic sell
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell another 1.67% today and is down 38.9% on what you paid. Lithium supply is recovering faster than demand right now, keeping prices soft. However, long-term outlooks to 2035 still project $15 billion in investment and record output — the structural story hasn't broken. This hurts to look at, but selling now would lock in the loss at the worst point. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — bouncing today, but still deeply underwater
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF had a good session today (+2.07%) on pre-earnings excitement for the big AI names. Still down 16.6% overall. With both GOOG and MSFT reporting tonight, GXAI could see follow-through movement tomorrow — in either direction. Long-term, AI is the right theme; the entry price was just a bit high. Hold.

watch_today.title: Gold smashing records at $4,075 USD — geopolitical fear driving it
watch_today.detail: Gold surged 1.63% last night to $4,075 USD per ounce — a record high. The main driver is escalating US-Iran conflict (9 nights of US strikes) and a global 'worldwide caution' advisory for US citizens. When fear spikes, investors pile into gold. You don't hold gold directly, but this signals broader risk-off sentiment that could affect your markets.

watch_today.title: Aussie dollar rising — a mixed signal for your US holdings
watch_today.detail: The AUD climbed to 70.2 US cents (+0.63%), its strongest level in a while. Good news for everyday life (cheaper imports, travel), but a rising AUD slightly reduces the AUD value of your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) when converted back. Nothing dramatic — just worth knowing.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict is escalating fast — 9 nights of American strikes and now Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Gold is at record highs on the fear. Elsewhere, Trump is fighting legal battles over voting rules, and the US FIFA World Cup wrapped up without a major security incident.

stories.title: US-Iran conflict escalates: 9 nights of strikes, Iran attacks Strait of Hormuz shipping
stories.why_it_matters: The United States has now conducted military strikes on Iran for nine consecutive nights, and Iran has responded by attacking ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most critical oil shipping lanes. Experts are warning the conflict risks spiralling out of control, with diplomatic efforts at a standstill. The Strait of Hormuz handles about 20% of global oil supply, so any serious disruption would push energy prices sharply higher worldwide — including petrol prices here in Australia. Gold hitting $4,075 USD per ounce (a record) reflects how worried markets are.

stories.title: US issues 'worldwide caution' warning for American citizens abroad
stories.why_it_matters: The US State Department issued a 'worldwide caution' alert for American travellers — essentially telling citizens everywhere abroad to be careful and stay alert to the possibility of retaliatory attacks related to the Iran conflict. Australia's SBS also warned Australians that the global security environment is 'unpredictable' right now. If you have travel plans overseas, it's worth checking your government's travel advisories. Travel insurance coverage may also be affected in active conflict zones.

stories.title: Trump wins temporary court victory on mail-in voting rules
stories.why_it_matters: A US federal appeals court handed the Trump administration a temporary win in its fight to restrict mail-in voting, while separately courts blocked Trump's push to access state voter rolls directly. These are ongoing legal battles over how the next US election will be run. Mail-in voting was a major flashpoint in 2020, and Trump has long sought to limit it. Separately, his effort to obtain state voter registration data — which critics say could be used for targeted voter suppression — hit a wall in the courts. US election integrity fights are heating up again ahead of the 2028 cycle.

stories.title: FIFA World Cup wraps up with zero major security incidents — FBI
stories.why_it_matters: The FBI has declared the 2026 FIFA World Cup — hosted across the US — a security success, citing zero major incidents across the entire tournament. Given the current global threat environment (US-Iran tensions, terror concerns), pulling off a major international event without a serious security breach is a genuine achievement. The tournament broke attendance and viewership records, giving the US a significant economic and soft-power win.

stories.title: USA-China-EU trade: fragmentation vs cooperation
stories.why_it_matters: Analysts are warning that the global trading system is splintering into competing blocs — the US, China, and the EU are all pulling in different directions on trade rules, tariffs, and technology. For Australia, which exports heavily to China and relies on US security alliances, this fragmentation is a serious long-term concern. It affects everything from commodity prices (iron ore, lithium) to the rules around tech companies operating here.

politics.summary: Two domestic stories today: the Albanese government is moving to limit how much AI can be used in automated government decisions, and union heavyweight Bill Kelty has taken a swing at Labor's push to reform cash transaction rules.

stories.title: Canberra to curb AI in automated government decision-making
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government is introducing new rules to limit how much automated AI systems can be used to make decisions that affect people — things like welfare payments, visa approvals, or tax assessments. The concern is that when an algorithm makes a decision with no human check, mistakes can be hard to appeal and can disproportionately hurt vulnerable people (think Robodebt, but with AI). The new rules would require meaningful human oversight for high-stakes government decisions. This is a significant policy move that puts Australia ahead of many comparable countries on AI governance.

stories.title: Union legend Bill Kelty attacks Labor's cash transaction reform push
stories.why_it_matters: Former ACTU secretary and union powerbroker Bill Kelty has publicly criticised the Albanese government's push to reform cash transaction rules — a plan that would limit how much cash businesses can accept without reporting it to authorities. Kelty's objections carry weight inside Labor given his historic influence with the union movement. Cash transaction reform is aimed at cracking down on the shadow economy and tax avoidance, but critics argue it unfairly targets small businesses and older Australians who prefer cash. The internal Labor pushback signals the reform may face a bumpy road.

ai.summary: The big AI story today is the race between Chinese and US models heating up — Chinese labs are closing the gap on OpenAI fast, while Google has delayed its next flagship Gemini model. Regulators worldwide are scrambling to keep up.

stories.title: Chinese AI models closing in on OpenAI — and Google's next big model is delayed
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese AI labs are rapidly catching up to the best American models — particularly OpenAI's GPT series — on benchmark tests that measure reasoning, coding, and knowledge. At the same time, Google has reportedly delayed the launch of Gemini 3.5 Pro, its next major AI model. This matters because the AI race is no longer a US-only contest: Chinese labs like Moonshot (Kimi K3) and Alibaba are now competitive at the frontier. For your GOOG and GXAI holdings, increased competition is worth watching — it means Google has less room to sit still.

stories.title: Alibaba launches new AI model to challenge Anthropic's Claude
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese tech giant Alibaba has launched a new AI model it claims can match or beat Anthropic's Claude (one of the best Western AI assistants). This follows Moonshot's Kimi K3 release. Chinese AI development is moving extremely fast — models that would have been state-of-the-art six months ago are already being challenged by newer Chinese entrants. For everyday users, more competition means better and cheaper AI tools. For investors in US AI companies, it means the moat (competitive advantage) is narrowing.

stories.title: Researchers warn: weak AI regulation may be worse than no regulation at all
stories.why_it_matters: A new research paper argues that half-baked AI regulation — rules that look tough but have major loopholes — can actually do more harm than no rules at all. The reason: weak rules give companies a 'compliance shield' (they can say they follow the rules) while still doing risky things. This is especially relevant as governments worldwide rush to be seen acting on AI without necessarily understanding it well enough to regulate effectively. Australia's new AI decision-making rules (see Politics) are an attempt to avoid this trap.

stories.title: US state attorneys general move on AI without waiting for federal rules
stories.why_it_matters: With the US Congress slow to pass any federal AI law, state attorneys general (the top law enforcement officers in each state) are stepping in using existing consumer protection and privacy laws to police AI companies. Several states have already launched investigations into AI chatbots, AI hiring tools, and AI in healthcare. This 'bottom-up' regulation through lawsuits and state laws creates a patchwork that AI companies operating in the US have to navigate carefully — adding compliance costs and legal risk for firms like Google and Microsoft.

markets.summary: The ASX barely moved today — up just 2 points — while last night on Wall Street the S&P 500 and NASDAQ slipped slightly ahead of major tech earnings. The big story in markets is gold surging to a record $4,075 USD on Iran-US conflict fears, and oil sliding as demand worries offset the geopolitical tension. The Aussie dollar pushed up to 70.2 US cents.

indicators.note: Essentially flat today — the market is holding its breath ahead of US earnings tonight.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw a small dip as investors stayed cautious ahead of major tech earnings from Alphabet and Microsoft.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Nearly flat last night — tech stocks edged lower overall despite gains in individual names like GOOG and MSFT.

indicators.name: Gold (USD/oz)
indicators.note: Record high — fear-driven buying on the back of US-Iran conflict escalating.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI, USD/bbl)
indicators.note: Oil dropped despite Middle East tensions — demand concerns are winning out for now, though Strait of Hormuz disruption risks remain.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is pushing back above 70 US cents, which slightly reduces the AUD value of your US holdings when converted.

sport.summary: NRL Round 21 kicks off Thursday with Eels v Panthers. The big team news is a major double blow for South Sydney — Latrell Mitchell is injured and coach Wayne Bennett faces a selection headache. AFL has a couple of notable stories too.

stories.title: South Sydney Rabbitohs hit with double injury blow ahead of Round 21
stories.why_it_matters: The Rabbitohs face a big selection crisis ahead of their Friday night clash against Melbourne Storm. Star fullback Latrell Mitchell has had an injury reveal that coach Wayne Bennett called a 'huge blow' — and there's a second injury concern on top of that. South Sydney host the Storm at Accor Stadium Friday at 8pm, and with Melbourne in top form, losing Latrell is a serious handicap. Bennett will need to reshuffle his back line significantly.

stories.title: NRL Round 21 team lists confirmed — every club's lineup
stories.why_it_matters: All Round 21 team lists are now confirmed. The round opens Thursday night with Eels v Panthers at CommBank Stadium (7:50pm). The Cowboys v Broncos Queensland derby on Saturday night (7:35pm at Queensland Country Bank Stadium in Townsville) is the marquee game for Gold Coast fans. Dolphins are on a bye this week.

stories.title: Melbourne Demons dump major sponsor over insurance claim denial
stories.why_it_matters: The Melbourne Demons have cut ties with a major club sponsor after the insurer denied an injury-related insurance claim. The specific details of the claim haven't been fully disclosed, but the Dees are clearly furious enough to pull the sponsorship publicly — a significant financial and reputational move by the club. It's a reminder that the business side of AFL clubs can be just as dramatic as what happens on the field.

stories.title: Collingwood's Nick Daicos a watch for AFL Round 18 — Pies sweating on star
stories.why_it_matters: Collingwood is nervously watching star midfielder Nick Daicos, who is listed as a concern heading into this week's AFL fixture. Meanwhile Melbourne has a 'major blow' with a key player in doubt — details suggest a breakout Demons player is potentially sidelined. The AFL season is entering a critical stretch where top teams can least afford to lose their best players to injury.
